newsitem.title: UK: Heating fuel strength keeps floor under oil price.
newsitem.headline: Heating fuel strength keeps floor under oil price.

text.p: World oil prices on Tuesday were little-changed from Monday's close as continued heating oil demand offset trader concerns about the possibility of a return of Iraqi oil exports.

The market recovered from earlier sharp lows sparked by Iraqi Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf's statement that he saw a consensus among foreign ministers at a United Nations General Assembly meeting for a speedy implementation of a deal allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil to pay for food and medicines.
At 1645 GMT, benchmark Brent November crude futures, which gained $1.50 last week, stood four cents up on the day at $23.25 but were well above Tuesday's low of $22.67.
Oil prices closed slightly slightly weaker on Monday as profit-taking and positive comments about the Iraqi "oil-for-food" deal by a top U.N. official stalled last week's rally.

Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said on Tuesday U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros Ghlai told her the oil pipeline carrying Iraqi crude to the Mediterranean via Turkey would reopen in a "few weeks."

But some traders wondered whether this was not just wishful thinking since it remains to be seen whether the United States and other U.N. Security Council members would not block implementation of the deal until the safety of U.N. inspectors in Iraq could be guaranteed.
Though Iraqi oil loomed bearishly in the background, heating oil's strength continued to lay a floor under prices.
In London October futures contract for gas oil, a middle distillate used in Europe as a heating fuel, peaked above $236 a tonne, their highest since the 1991 Gulf War.

Heating oil prices could get a further boost if a weekly report on U.S. primary oil stock levels, released after the market close by the American Petroleum Institute (API), shows heating oil inventories are still way below 1995 levels.
"Fundamental demand keeps filtering through. There's been some second-guessing on the APIs," said broker Alistair Harris of MeesPierson Derivatives.

But further gains were hampered by talk of the delayed oil-for-food sale, reminding traders that as much as 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi oil exports could hit the market once the deal is implemented.

Oil analysts had expected to see as early as this month the first Iraqi oil exports in more than six years after Baghdad was hit by crippling sanctions. But the plan was suspended when President Saddam Hussein sent troops into Kurdish areas in northern Iraq at the beginning of September.
